posts.title: Testing the Unpredictable: Agentic AI, n8n, and AI Security
posts.author: Surafel Kindu
posts.excerpt: Notes from my day-to-day as a software engineer at TestSavant.AI — testing agentic AI systems that never give the same answer twice, wiring it all together with n8n, and probing AI for security holes before attackers do.

blocks.text: Traditional software is polite: same input, same output, every time. AI applications are not. At TestSavant.AI, where I work as a software engineer, my job is to help teams test, harden and prove systems that are non-deterministic by design — agentic workflows, RAG pipelines and chatbots that can give a different answer on every run.
Agentic AI breaks the old QA playbook

An agent doesn't just return text — it plans, calls tools and takes actions. That means a test can't just check 'was the answer good?' It has to ask: did the agent capture every action it should? Did it call the right tool with schema-valid arguments? Can it be tricked into leaking its system prompt? These are the failure modes I think about every day, and each one needs its own evaluator.

The interesting engineering challenge is that generic test cases are useless here. A test suite has to be specific to the application under test, and it has to concentrate on the categories where that application is actually weakest — otherwise you're burning tokens to feel safe.
Where n8n fits in

n8n has become my favorite glue. Testing AI once is easy; testing it continuously is the real product. I use n8n to orchestrate the boring-but-critical plumbing around evaluation runs so that quality checks happen without anyone remembering to click a button.

items: Scheduled regression runs that fire daily or on every model/prompt update
CI/CD release gates — a failing run blocks the release like any pipeline check
Failure alerts routed to the right channel with the category and policy label attached
Evidence reports generated and delivered after every run

blocks.text: The pattern that works: keep the workflow dumb and the evaluators smart. n8n moves data and triggers runs; the evaluators decide what 'good' means.
AI security is not optional

The other half of my work is adversarial. AI red teaming means probing a system the way an attacker would: prompt injection to hijack instructions, attempts to extract the system prompt, nudging the model to leak PII or confidential data, pushing it off-topic or into answers your sources don't support.

What I like about this space is that testing and protection form a loop: red teaming finds the failure, runtime guardrails enforce the fix in production, re-runs confirm the fix holds, and every cycle leaves evidence you can hand to a CTO or a compliance team.
You can't ship what you can't test — and you can't secure what you never probe.
What I've learned so far

items: Evals must be application-specific — generic LLM-generated tests miss your real risks
Test at every level: the live UI, the agent workflow, the system prompt, and the raw model
Track failure rates run over run — a slow decline is a regression too
Guardrails and testing are one loop, not two products
Every release needs evidence, not vibes

blocks.text: If you're building agentic or RAG applications and your testing strategy is 'we tried it a few times and it looked fine' — I have been there, and I promise the failure rate will surprise you. Feel free to reach out; this is literally my day job.

posts.title: Halt: One Rate-Limiting Policy for Every Stack I Touch
posts.author: Surafel Kindu
posts.excerpt: Why I built Halt — an open-source rate-limiting SDK with safe defaults, observability hooks and distributed storage, working the same in Python and TypeScript.

blocks.text: Every API I have ever shipped eventually needed rate limiting — and every time, the answer was a different library, tied to a different framework, with different defaults and different header conventions. Halt is the tool I wanted instead: one policy language, drop-in middleware, working the same in Python and TypeScript.
Middleware, not homework

Halt sits between your clients and your handlers. It identifies who is calling (by IP, user, API key — your strategy), counts their requests against a policy, and forwards or blocks each one in well under a millisecond. Your route code never changes.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from halt import RateLimiter, InMemoryStore, presets
from halt.adapters.fastapi import HaltMiddleware

app = FastAPI()

limiter = RateLimiter(
    store=InMemoryStore(),
    policy=presets.PUBLIC_API  # 100 req/min
)

app.add_middleware(HaltMiddleware, limiter=limiter)
Blocked requests get a 429 before your handler ever runs, every response carries RateLimit-* headers, and well-behaved clients get a Retry-After so they can back off on their own.
One policy, any stack

Halt ships with four algorithms (Token Bucket, Fixed Window, Sliding Window, Leaky Bucket), six storage backends (Memory, Redis, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Memcached), and adapters for eight frameworks — FastAPI, Flask, Django, Litestar, Starlette on the Python side; Express, NestJS, Next.js, Hono, Fastify on the TypeScript side.

blocks.caption: One policy. Any stack. Limit with confidence.

blocks.text: Built for SaaS from day one

items: Plans, quotas and penalties — free tier vs team tier with per-plan tagging
Weighted endpoints so expensive routes cost more of the budget
Health-check exemptions and private-IP allowlists out of the box
StatsCollector for a /halt/stats endpoint plus an OpenTelemetry metrics adapter
Burst-friendly algorithms like Token Bucket that refill gradually

blocks.caption: Drop-in middleware with safe defaults and observability hooks.

blocks.text: Halt is open source (github.com/surafel-kindu/halt) and currently at v0.4.0 — production-ready, but early. More framework adapters, more storage backends and deeper SaaS tooling are on the roadmap.

pip install halt-rate
# or
npm install halt-rate
If you try it, open an issue with what broke — that's how it's gotten this far.
